literal: The Han followed Qin institutions: the emperor's paternal grandmother was styled Grand Empress Dowager, his mother Empress Dowager, his principal consort Empress; the rest were mostly called Lady, increased or reduced with the age—not like the Rites of Zhou with fixed numbers of ladies, concubines, wives, and palace women.
idiomatic: Under the Han, who took over Qin practice, the emperor's grandmother was Grand Empress Dowager, his mother Empress Dowager, and his chief consort Empress; everyone else was usually called Lady, with titles shifting over time rather than the fixed ranks of lady, concubine, wife, and palace woman set out in the Rites of Zhou.

literal: Wei and Jin carried this on, with promotions and demotions from time to time; earlier histories have set it out fully.
idiomatic: Wei and Jin inherited the same system, raising and lowering ranks as times changed; earlier histories already tell that story in full.

literal: Though the omen of Wei royal enterprise began with Shenyuan, down to before Emperor Zhaocheng the age prized austerity; consorts, concubines, and palace women were mostly lacking, and only order of precedence served as title.
idiomatic: The Wei kings' mandate may have begun with Shenyuan, but until the reign before Emperor Zhaocheng the court prized plain living: few consorts or palace women are recorded, and women were known only by their rank in the sequence.

literal: Yet for the eight rulers Emperor Zhang, Emperor Ping, Emperor Si, Emperor Zhao, Emperor Mu, Emperor Hui, Emperor Yang, and Emperor Lie, no empress or consort is heard of.
idiomatic: For eight early rulers—Zhang, Ping, Si, Zhao, Mu, Hui, Yang, and Lie—no empress or consort is named at all.

literal: Taizu posthumously honored his forebears' wives, all taking the emperor's posthumous title as empress; the central palace was first established; other women might be called Lady, without limit in number, yet all had grades.
idiomatic: Taizu raised his ancestors' wives to empress in posthumous title, established the central palace, and allowed other women the title Lady in unlimited number, each with a defined rank.

literal: Shizu gradually added Left and Right Worthy Ladies, Honored Persons, Pepper Chamber, Central Style, and several other ranks; the rear palace grew numerous.
idiomatic: Shizu gradually added left and right worthy ladies, honored persons, pepper-chamber attendants, central-style ranks, and the like, and the rear palace swelled.

literal: By Wei precedent, before establishing an empress she had to cast a golden figure by hand; success was auspicious, failure meant she could not be enthroned.
idiomatic: Wei custom required a woman to cast a gold figure with her own hands before she could be made empress: success meant good fortune; failure barred the throne.

literal: Again, Shizu and Gaozong, moved by wet-nurses' toil and care, both showed the utmost honor—though the acts breached ritual, one may see benevolence through the fault.
idiomatic: Shizu and Gaozong both lavished honor on their wet-nurses out of gratitude for exhausting care; the practice broke ritual, yet the kindness behind the breach is plain.

literal: Gaozu reformed the inner offices: Left and Right Worthy Ladies ranked with the Grand Marshal; Three Ladies with the Three Excellencies; Three Consorts with the three ministers; Six Consorts with the six ministers; World Wives with palace grand masters; Palace Women with chief clerks.
idiomatic: Gaozu reorganized the inner court: left and right worthy ladies equaled the grand marshal; three ladies the three excellencies; three consorts the three ministers; six consorts the six ministers; world wives palace grand masters; palace women chief clerks.

literal: Later female offices were added to administer inner affairs.
idiomatic: Later he added female offices to run palace affairs.

literal: The Inner Director ranked with the Directors of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: The inner director ranked with the directors of the Masters of Writing.

literal: The Director of Works, Grand Supervisor, and Female Palace Attendant—the three offices—ranked at the second grade.
idiomatic: Director of works, grand supervisor, and female palace attendant—the three posts—held second-grade rank.

literal: Supervisor, Female Master of Writing, Beauty, Female Scribe, Female Worthy, Book Scribe, Book Woman, and Junior Book Woman—the five offices—ranked at the third grade.
idiomatic: Supervisor, female master of writing, beauty, female scribe, female worthy, book scribe, book woman, and junior book woman—five offices—held third-grade rank.

literal: Central Talented Woman, Attendant, Central Palace Maid, Talented Woman, and Respectful Palace Woman ranked at the fourth grade; Spring Robe, Wine Woman, Feast Woman, Food Woman, and Palace Slave ranked at the fifth.
idiomatic: Central talented woman, attendant, central palace maid, talented woman, and respectful palace woman were fourth grade; spring robe, wine woman, feast woman, food woman, and palace slave were fifth.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Empress of Shenyuan, Lady Dou, was daughter of Bin, paramount chief of the Moluhui tribe.
idiomatic: Empress of Shenyuan, née Dou, was the daughter of Bin, paramount chief of the Moluhui tribe.

literal: As Bin lay dying he admonished his two sons Suho and Huiti to serve the emperor well.
idiomatic: On his deathbed Bin warned his sons Suho and Huiti to serve the emperor faithfully.

literal: When Bin died, Suho and the others wished to use the emperor's attendance at the funeral to raise a revolt; word leaked somewhat; the emperor heard and, knowing they would never submit, moved against them first.
idiomatic: After Bin's death Suho and his brothers planned a coup when the emperor came to the funeral; word leaked; the emperor knew they would never submit and struck first.

literal: He then hid warriors in the palace; at dawn he killed the empress with his belt knife, sent a fast rider to tell Suho and the rest that the empress had died suddenly.
idiomatic: Warriors lay hidden in the palace; at dawn the emperor killed the empress with his belt knife and sent riders to Suho saying she had died suddenly.

literal: Suho and the others, alarmed, rushed to attend; he seized and killed them.
idiomatic: Suho and his brothers ran to the palace in alarm and were seized and killed.

literal: Empress of Emperor Wen, Lady Feng, bore Emperors Huan and Mu and died young.
idiomatic: Emperor Wen's empress, née Feng, bore Emperors Huan and Mu and died young.

literal: When Emperor Huan took the throne she was buried.
idiomatic: When Emperor Huan was enthroned, she was buried at last.

literal: [3] Early in Gaozong's reign, while digging the Tianyuan Pool, a stone inscription was found saying Emperor Huan buried his mother Lady Feng; more than two hundred thousand came from near and far to the gathering.
idiomatic: [3] Early in Gaozong's reign workers digging the Tianyuan Pool found a stone inscription recording that Emperor Huan buried his mother Lady Feng; more than two hundred thousand people gathered from near and far.

literal: The responsible offices reported; he ordered it stored in the Grand Temple.
idiomatic: The court reported the find; the emperor ordered the stone kept in the Grand Temple.

literal: The next consort, Lady Lan, bore two sons; the elder was called Lan and died young;
idiomatic: A secondary consort, Lady Lan, bore two sons; the elder, named Lan, died young;

literal: the younger was Emperor Si.
idiomatic: the younger became Emperor Si.

literal: Empress of Emperor Huan, Lady Qi, [4] bore three sons: the eldest Pugen, next Emperor Hui, next Emperor Yang.
idiomatic: Emperor Huan's empress, née Qi, [4] bore three sons: Pugen the eldest, then Emperor Hui, then Emperor Yang.

literal: When Emperor Pingwen died the empress held state affairs; people called it a women's realm.
idiomatic: When Emperor Pingwen died the empress governed; people spoke of a women's state.

literal: The empress was fierce and jealous; Emperor Pingwen's death was her doing.
idiomatic: She was fierce and jealous; Emperor Pingwen's death was her work.

literal: Empress of Emperor Pingwen, Lady Wang, was a native of Guangning.
idiomatic: Emperor Pingwen's empress, née Wang, came from Guangning.

literal: At thirteen she entered the palace on business and won Emperor Pingwen's favor, bearing Emperor Zhaocheng.
idiomatic: At thirteen she entered the palace on an errand, won Emperor Pingwen's favor, and bore Emperor Zhaocheng.

literal: When Emperor Pingwen died, Zhaocheng was still in swaddling clothes.
idiomatic: When Emperor Pingwen died, Zhaocheng was still an infant in swaddling clothes.

literal: The state then had internal strife and men meant to kill the princes.
idiomatic: Civil strife broke out; plotters meant to kill the princes.

literal: The empress hid the emperor in her trousers, fearing discovery, and prayed: "If Heaven's mandate is not ended, be silent.
idiomatic: She hid the child in her trousers and prayed, fearing discovery: "If Heaven's mandate is not ended, be silent."

literal: " For a long time he did not cry and escaped harm.
idiomatic: " He did not cry for a long time and was spared.

literal: When Zhaocheng first wished to fix the capital at the Luanyuan River, build walls, and raise palaces, deliberation did not decide.
idiomatic: When Emperor Zhaocheng first planned to settle on the Luanyuan River, build walls, and raise palaces, the court could not agree.

literal: The empress heard and said: "From high antiquity our state has made migration its calling.
idiomatic: The empress objected: "From antiquity this people has lived by migration.

literal: Now, after hardship, the foundation is not firm.
idiomatic: After recent troubles the foundation is still weak.

literal: If we dwell within walls, when raiders come we cannot move at once.
idiomatic: If we build walled towns and enemies strike, we cannot flee at once."

literal: He stopped.
idiomatic: The plan was abandoned.

literal: When Emperor Lie died the throne was nearly lost; the great revival was her work.
idiomatic: When Emperor Lie died the dynasty nearly perished; she did the work of revival.

literal: In the eighteenth year she died and was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.
idiomatic: She died in the eighteenth year and was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.

literal: When Taizu took the throne she was paired in sacrifice at the Grand Temple.
idiomatic: When Taizu took the throne she received paired sacrifice in the Grand Temple.

literal: Empress Xianming, Lady He, had as father Yegan, paramount chief of the Eastern Division.
idiomatic: Empress Xianming, née He—her father Yegan was paramount chief of the Eastern Division.

literal: The empress in youth was chosen into the Eastern Palace for beauty and bore Taizu.
idiomatic: Chosen young into the eastern palace for her looks, she bore Taizu.

literal: When Fu Luo raided within the borders, the empress fled north with Taizu and former ministers and clerks.
idiomatic: When Fu Luo invaded, she fled north with Taizu and loyal officials.

literal: Soon the Gaoche came raiding; the empress rode in a cart with Taizu fleeing south from the bandits.
idiomatic: Soon Gaoche raiders struck; she rode south with Taizu to escape them.

literal: Midway the axle broke; the empress in fear looked to Heaven and said: "The imperial line—can it end with us alone!
idiomatic: Midway the axle broke. She looked up in terror and cried: "Can the imperial line end with us alone!

literal: Only let the spirits aid us.
idiomatic: Spirits, aid us!"

literal: They galloped on; the wheel held straight and did not tip.
idiomatic: They galloped on; the wheel held true and did not tip.

literal: After more than a hundred li they reached the south of Mount Qijie and escaped harm.
idiomatic: After more than a hundred li they reached the south slope of Mount Qijie and were safe.

literal: Later Liu Xian sent men to kill Taizu; the emperor's aunt was wife to Xian's brother Kangnuili and knew; she secretly told the empress; Liang Juan also came to warn of danger.
idiomatic: Later Liu Xian sent men to kill Taizu. The emperor's aunt, married to Xian's brother Kangnuili, learned of it and warned the empress in secret; Liang Juan brought the same warning.

literal: The empress then had Taizu leave.
idiomatic: She sent Taizu away at once.

literal: At night the empress made Xian's envoy drunk.
idiomatic: That night she plied Xian's envoy with wine until he was drunk.

literal: Toward dawn she deliberately startled the stable horses; the envoy rose to look at the horses.
idiomatic: Before dawn she stampeded the stable horses; the envoy rose to inspect them.

literal: The empress wept and said: "All my sons were here; now they are all gone.
idiomatic: Weeping, she said: "All my sons were here; now they have vanished.

literal: Which of you killed them?
idiomatic: Which of you killed them?"

literal: Thus Xian's men did not pursue in haste.
idiomatic: Xian's men did not pursue in haste.

literal: [5] Taizu reached the Helan tribe; the people's hearts had not yet fully turned to him; the empress's cousin Yue, outer-court grandee, led his whole tribe to follow and served with full ritual.
idiomatic: [5] When Taizu reached the Helan tribe hearts were not yet won; the empress's cousin Yue, an outer-court grandee, led his whole tribe to follow and served with full ceremony.

literal: Xian was enraged and meant to kill the empress; she fled by night to Kangnuili's house and hid three days in the spirit cart; Kangnuili's whole household begged for her life and she was spared.
idiomatic: Xian raged and meant to kill her; she fled by night to Kangnuili's house and hid three days in the spirit cart until his household begged for her life.

literal: When Liu Xian's tribe fell into disorder she at last escaped home.
idiomatic: When Liu Xian's tribe fell into disorder she escaped home at last.

literal: Later the empress's brother Ran'gan, jealous that Taizu had won hearts, raised troops and besieged the traveling palace; the empress came out and said to Ran'gan: "Where will you place me now, yet you mean to kill my son?
idiomatic: Later her brother Ran'gan, jealous of Taizu's popularity, besieged the traveling palace. The empress confronted him: "Where will you put me, if you kill my son?"

literal: Ran'gan left in shame.
idiomatic: Ran'gan withdrew in shame.

literal: Empress of Emperor Daowu, Lady Murong, was the youngest daughter of Murong Bao.
idiomatic: Emperor Daowu's empress, née Murong, was Murong Bao's youngest daughter.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified she entered the rear palace and won favor.
idiomatic: When Zhongshan fell she entered the rear palace and won favor.

literal: Left Chancellor Prince Wei of the Guard and others memorialized to establish an empress; the emperor followed the ministers' counsel, ordered the empress to cast a golden figure; it succeeded and she was enthroned, with announcement at the suburban altars.
idiomatic: Prince Wei of the Guard, left chancellor, and others asked that she be made empress. The emperor agreed, had her cast the gold figure; it succeeded, and she was enthroned with rites at the suburban altars.

literal: He enfeoffed the empress's mother Lady Meng as Lady of Piaoyang.
idiomatic: He enfeoffed her mother Lady Meng as Lady of Piaoyang.

literal: [6] Later she died.
idiomatic: [6] She died later.

literal: Empress Xuanmu of Emperor Daowu, Lady Liu, was daughter of Liu Juan.
idiomatic: Emperor Daowu's Empress Xuanmu, née Liu, was Liu Juan's daughter.

literal: At the beginning of Dengguo she was taken as Lady and bore the Princess of Huayin, later Taizong.
idiomatic: At the start of Dengguo she became a lady and bore the Princess of Huayin, later Taizong.

literal: The empress managed inner affairs exclusively and received added favor; because the golden figure did not succeed she could not ascend to empress.
idiomatic: She ran inner affairs alone and was deeply favored, but the gold figure failed and she never became empress.

literal: By Wei precedent, when the rear palace bore a son who would be heir apparent, the mother was ordered to die.
idiomatic: Wei custom required the mother of an heir apparent to die.

literal: In Taizu's last years the empress died by the old law.
idiomatic: In Taizu's last years she died under that old law.

literal: When Taizong took the throne he raised her posthumous title and paired her in the Grand Temple.
idiomatic: When Taizong took the throne he gave her a posthumous title and paired her in the Grand Temple.

literal: From then on every rear-palace woman who was the emperor's mother took the principal place in paired sacrifice.
idiomatic: After that every emperor's mother from the rear palace took the principal place in paired sacrifice.

literal: Empress Zhaogong of Emperor Mingyuan, Lady Yao, was daughter of Yao Xing; Xing enfeoffed her Princess of Xiping.
idiomatic: Emperor Mingyuan's Empress Zhaogong, née Yao, was Yao Xing's daughter; Xing made her Princess of Xiping.

literal: Taizong received her with empress rites; later she was Lady.
idiomatic: Taizong received her with empress ceremony; later she held the rank of lady.

literal: Because the golden figure did not succeed she did not rise to supreme rank, yet the emperor favored her; coming and going, dwelling and rank were as for an empress.
idiomatic: The gold figure failed and she never took supreme rank, yet the emperor favored her as if she were empress in residence and ceremony.

literal: Afterward he still wished to establish her, but the empress declined as unfitting.
idiomatic: He still wished to make her empress, but she declined as unfitting.

literal: In the fifth year of Taichang she died; the emperor mourned with regret, bestowed empress seal and sash, and added a posthumous title.
idiomatic: She died in the fifth year of Taichang; the emperor mourned, gave her empress seal and sash, and added a posthumous title.

literal: She was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.
idiomatic: She was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.

literal: Secret Empress of Emperor Mingyuan, Lady Du, was a native of Ye in Wei commandery, sister to Prince Chao of Yangping.
idiomatic: Emperor Mingyuan's Secret Empress, née Du, came from Ye in Wei commandery; she was sister to Prince Chao of Yangping.

literal: At first, as a woman of good family, she was chosen into the crown prince's palace, won favor, and bore Shizu.
idiomatic: Chosen as a woman of good family into the crown prince's palace, she won favor and bore Shizu.

literal: When Taizong took the throne she was made Honored Consort.
idiomatic: When Taizong took the throne she became honored consort.

literal: In the fifth year of Taichang she died; posthumous title Secret Honored Consort; burial at Jinling in Yunzhong.
idiomatic: She died in the fifth year of Taichang with the posthumous title Secret Honored Consort and was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.

literal: When Shizu took the throne he raised her posthumous title and paired her in the Grand Temple.
idiomatic: At Shizu's accession he raised her posthumous title and gave her paired sacrifice in the Grand Temple.

literal: He also built an empress temple at Ye; the provincial governor offered seasonal sacrifice.
idiomatic: He also built an empress temple at Ye, where the provincial governor offered seasonal sacrifice.

literal: Because it was the home commandery of the Great Empress Dowager's birth, corvée and levies there were remitted.
idiomatic: Because it was the empress dowager's native commandery, corvée and levies there were remitted.

literal: Later sweet dew fell in the temple courtyard.
idiomatic: Later sweet dew fell in the temple courtyard.

literal: In Gaozu's time, [7] the provincial governor of Xiangzhou, Gao Lü, memorialized to repair the empress temple; an edict said: "Women achieve completion outward; in principle they are not sacrificed alone; yin must be paired with yang to complete Heaven and Earth; one has not heard of a temple to Tai Si in the state of Youxin.
idiomatic: In Gaozu's time, [7] Gao Lü, governor of Xiangzhou, asked to repair the empress temple. The edict said: "Women find completion outside the family; they are not sacrificed alone; yin must pair with yang to make Heaven and Earth whole. No one has heard of a separate feast for Tai Si in the state of Youxin.

literal: This was what the late emperor established—a moment's utmost feeling, not a far-reaching institutional rule; the sacrifices may cease."
idiomatic: This was the late emperor's moment of feeling, not eternal law; let the separate sacrifices cease."

literal: Empress of Emperor Taiwu, Lady Helian, was daughter of Helian Qubuq.
idiomatic: Emperor Taiwu's empress, née Helian, was Helian Qubuq's daughter.

literal: When Shizu pacified Tongwan he took the empress and two younger sisters as honored persons; later she was made empress.
idiomatic: When Shizu took Tongwan he made the empress and her two younger sisters honored persons; later she became empress.

literal: When Gaozong first died she was associated in burial at Jinling.
idiomatic: When Gaozong first died she was associated in burial at Jinling.

literal: Empress Jing'ai of Emperor Taiwu, Lady He, was a native of Dai.
idiomatic: Emperor Taiwu's Empress Jing'ai, née He, came from Dai.

literal: At first she was Lady and bore Gongzong.
idiomatic: At first she was a lady and bore Gongzong.

literal: In the first year of Shenju she died; posthumously made Honored Consort; burial at Jinling in Yunzhong.
idiomatic: She died in the first year of Shenju, was posthumously made honored consort, and was buried at Jinling in Yunzhong.

literal: Later her title and posthumous name were added and she was paired in the Grand Temple.
idiomatic: Later her title was raised and she was paired in the Grand Temple.

literal: Empress Gong of Jingmu, Lady Yujiulü, was sister to Prince Pi of Hedong.
idiomatic: Jingmu's Empress Gong, née Yujiulü, was sister to Prince Pi of Hedong.

literal: In youth she was chosen into the Eastern Palace and won favor.
idiomatic: Chosen young into the eastern palace, she won favor.
